Take the detour. The main thread keeps going.

macOS · No account needed to run locally · Chats stored on your machine

Michi is a desktop workspace that runs Claude Code, Codex, Kiro and Pi. Select any sentence in an agent’s reply and branch it into its own pane. It starts with everything above it, runs beside the main thread, and nothing comes back until you choose.

A subagent runs an errand. A branch explores an idea.

Diagram. Left: a subagent’s errand loops out of the main thread to one task, check identity 7, which turns done; the loop returns and fades, and only its result stays on the main thread. Right: a branch leaves the main thread and keeps going with its own steps, Why Tokyo only? and A timing gap, while the main thread continues to the post-deploy checks.

Multi-agent tools scale execution. Michi scales direction.

You decide what splits off, what keeps going and what comes back. The agents do the work inside each branch.

Every branch starts with everything above it. Nothing leaks back up.

The branch gets the question and the answer up to the words you picked. Whatever the main thread says next stays there, until you merge it or @ it.

Every branch is a whole conversation. Open more, go back for a second round, pull in what it found.

Ask the agent to branch.

Say “Branch both leads.” You get one branch per lead, both working. They wait at the edge of the strip, so nothing steals your focus.

A second round, not a new chat.

Comment on exact lines and send them together. The branch takes your constraints and changes its answer.

@ a branch or an artifact.

Pull what a branch found, or a saved doc, into your next prompt. Nothing else comes back.

Animated example in three steps.

First, in the main thread, they type “Branch both leads. My guess is a stale account.” The agent opens two branches, Identity check and Why Tokyo only?, which wait at the edge of the strip.

Second, in Identity check, the branch has found all 11 developer accounts valid and the task runner role missing, and suggests dropping the role from the policy. They answer its three questions with comments: keep every permission, change Tokyo only, and count a retry as a deploy plus a clean startup. They send the comments together, and the branch changes its answer: create the role in Tokyo before the policy runs.

Third, back in the main thread, they ask it to update the saved post-deploy checks with what Identity check found, and two checks are added.

See how you got here. Merge the branches that matter.

The Map shows every branch and where it came from. Select a few and merge them into a new thread. The originals stay as they were, and you can still @ any of them.

A month later, just ask. It reads the whole tree back, dead ends included.

Threads are kept. Ask a new chat how you fixed it, and the agent reads the branches back: what you ruled out, what caused it, and what is still unverified.

Step away. The workspace keeps up. It writes its home page, keeps the notes you give it, runs prompts on a schedule, and opens on your phone.

A home page that writes itself.

The Meta agent reads each conversation you finish and keeps the workspace’s page current. Each item links back to the message it came from, and if you edited a block, it asks before changing it.

Tell it once. Every agent knows.

Michi keeps the note and hands it to whichever agent you pick next: Claude Code, Codex, Kiro or Pi. Every note is listed in Settings, where you can change or delete it.

Prompts on a schedule.

Ask the Meta agent for a weekday check and approve the job it drafts. Each run lands in a thread you can pick up, and Michi tells you when it’s done.

Pick it up on your phone.

Point a workspace at a machine you run, and its turns keep going after you close the laptop. The same machine can serve your threads to your phone.

Animated example in four parts.

First, the tokyo-rollout home page in Pages. The Meta agent reads a conversation that just finished and adds a Cause block: the permissions policy runs before bootstrap creates the task runner role. The block’s Sources button opens the message it came from, in Tokyo deployment RCA, with Continue this chat. The rollout is still paused, with validation pending.

Second, in Tokyo deployment, they type “Remember for this project: change Tokyo only and keep every existing permission.” The agent searches its memory, saves the note and replies “Saved for tokyo-rollout.”, and Michi shows “Remembered” with Undo. Then, in a new chat with Codex, they ask “Draft the Tokyo fix.” With no memory tool call, the answer keeps to Tokyo and every existing permission: create the task runner role in Tokyo before the policy runs, and leave the other regions unchanged.

Third, on the Scheduled page, the weekday job Tokyo deploy check is due and runs. When it finishes, its next run is a day away and a desktop notification says: Check 4 failed: the task runner role is still missing in Tokyo. Rollout stays paused.

Fourth, the tokyo-rollout workspace runs on a remote machine. The desktop dims and a phone opens the Tokyo deployment thread, with both branches still working. They open the pane list and pick Identity check, which has finished its first round: all 11 developer accounts are valid, and the task runner role is missing in Tokyo.

Runs the agents you already use. Your chats stay on your machine.

Agents
Claude Code, Codex, Kiro and Pi. Pick one per conversation, with its own model and permission mode.
Permissions
Ask before changes, Trust inside the agent’s sandbox, or YOLO where the agent supports it. Per chat or for everything.
Your chats
Stored in a SQLite database on your machine. No account needed to run locally.
Prompts
Each agent sends your prompts to its own provider.
Code
Every branch works in the same project folder. No git branches, no worktrees, no code isolation. Files change only when an agent edits them, with your permission.
Closing a pane
Never deletes history or stops a running turn. Reopen it and the turn picks up.
Remote
Optional. Point a workspace at a machine you run, over SSH. Its turns keep running there after you close the app, and that machine can serve your threads to your phone.
Platform
macOS, for now.

Questions people ask first.

Is this another multi-agent orchestrator?

No. Orchestrators split one task across agents that report back and end. In Michi you open each branch yourself, keep talking to it for as many rounds as it needs, and decide what comes back. It can run on the same agents.

Does a branch create a git branch or a worktree?

No. A branch is a conversation, not a checkout. Every branch works in the same project folder, so Michi doesn’t isolate code changes.

What does a branch know?

Everything above the sentence you branched from, plus anything you @-mention. Nothing leaks back up until you merge it or @ it.

Does merging change the branches?

No. Merge starts a new thread from the branches you picked. The originals stay exactly as they were.

Where does my data live?

In a SQLite database on your Mac. You don’t need a Michi account to run it locally. Each agent still talks to its own provider.

Why not a new chat, or tmux?

A new chat starts from nothing, and a tmux split is another terminal. A branch starts with the exact context it came from, and Michi keeps the whole tree.

What does Memory keep?

Only the notes you ask for or approve: preferences, facts, decisions and conventions, for every workspace or just one. They’re stored with your chats on your machine, every agent reads them, and you can change or delete any of them in Settings.
